# keel: a dependency resolver and lock validator

`keel` reads a package index, a project file and (optionally) a lock file from the **current directory**, decides which version of which package to use, and writes or checks a lock file. The version scheme, the constraint syntax and the way conflicts are searched are specific to this ecosystem; follow the rules below, not the conventions of any real package manager.

Build and run it as `target/debug/keel`, built with `cargo build --offline` (binary crate `keel`, entry point `src/main.rs`, no dependencies). Usage: `keel COMMAND [ARGS]`. Everything is printed to standard output (nothing on standard error matters). The exit status is `1` if any printed line starts with `error:` or `FAILED`, otherwise `0`.

## 1. Words, names, versions

Files are read as lines of text. In every file `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line; the rest of a line is split into *words* at white space; lines without words are skipped. Line numbers start at 1 and count every line, comments and empty lines included.

A **name** is a lower-case letter followed by lower-case letters, digits and `-` (package names, feature names, nothing else).

A **version** is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` where each number is `0` or has no leading zero and at most six digits, optionally followed by `-TAG`, a **tag** being one or more lower-case letters followed by digits (for example `rc1`, `beta12`). Versions are ordered by the three numbers; for equal numbers a version *with* a tag is lower than the one without, and two tags are compared as plain byte strings (`rc10` < `rc2`). Two versions are equal when they are equal in that order.

## 2. Constraints

A **constraint** is one word (no spaces): clauses separated by `,`, and a version must satisfy every clause. A clause is an operator and a *partial version* (`1`, `1.2` or `1.2.3`, or `1.2.3-rc1`; missing numbers count as 0; a tag requires all three numbers), or `*`, or a bare partial version, which means `=` (always allowed). Clause meanings (`V` is the partial version completed with zeros):

* `>=V`: at least `V`
* `>V`: greater than `V`
* `<=V`: at most `V`
* `<V`: less than `V`
* `=V`: equal to `V`
* `!=V`: not equal to `V`
* `^V`: at least `V` and below the *next breaking number*: `(MAJOR+1).0.0` if MAJOR is not 0; `0.(MINOR+1).0` if MAJOR is 0 and MINOR is not 0; `0.0.(PATCH+1)` if both are 0
* `~V`: at least `V` and below `MAJOR.(MINOR+1).0`
* `*`: every version

The upper bound of `^` and `~` is compared on the three numbers only, whatever the tag: a version is below the bound when its triple is (so `^1.2` allows `1.9.9-rc1` but not `2.0.0-rc1`). All other clause comparisons (`>=`, `<`, `=` and so on) use the full version order of section 1, so `<2.0.0` *does* allow `2.0.0-rc1` and `>=1.0.0` does not allow `1.0.0-rc1`. A constraint that is empty, has an empty clause, an unknown operator or a bad partial version is a **bad constraint**.

## 3. The files

**`index.txt`** lists the available packages as blocks. A block starts with `pkg NAME VERSION` and continues with directive lines until the next `pkg` line:

* `needs NAME CONSTRAINT [+FEATURE...] [if FEATURE]`: this package version needs the package `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT`. `+FEATURE` words ask for features of `NAME` to be enabled. `if FEATURE` makes the need *conditional*: it is only active when `FEATURE` of this package is enabled (the feature must have been declared earlier in the same block).
* `feature NAME`: this version offers the feature `NAME` (declaring a feature twice in a block is an error).
* `breaks NAME CONSTRAINT`: this version cannot be used together with any version of `NAME` that satisfies `CONSTRAINT`.
* `yanked`: this version is withdrawn: it is never chosen, unless the lock file already holds exactly this version (see `lock`).

The same package may appear in several blocks with different versions; the same name and version twice is an error.

**`project.txt`** has one directive per line: `want NAME CONSTRAINT [+FEATURE...]`: the project needs `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT` with the given features enabled. Several lines may mention the same name.

**`lock.txt`** has one line per locked package, sorted by name: `NAME VERSION [FEATURES]`, where `FEATURES` is one word: the enabled features sorted by name and joined with `,` (omitted when none is enabled).

**File errors.** A file that cannot be read gives `error: cannot read FILE`. A malformed line gives `error: FILE:LINE: MESSAGE` and nothing else is done; the first problem in file order wins. `MESSAGE` is one of:

* `unknown directive 'WORD'` (first word not allowed in that file; the allowed ones are `pkg`, `needs`, `yanked`, `breaks`, `feature` in the index and `want` in the project);
* `'WORD' outside a package block` (an index directive before the first `pkg` line);
* `bad line` (wrong number of words for the directive; in `needs` and `want` the `+FEATURE` words come after the constraint);
* `bad name 'X'` (checked after the shape: the package name of `pkg`/`needs`/`breaks`/`want`, the gate of `if`, each feature of `feature` and `+FEATURE`, `X` printed without the `+`);
* `bad version 'V'`, `bad constraint 'C'` (checked after the names of the same line);
* `duplicate package NAME VERSION`, `duplicate feature 'F'`, `undeclared feature 'F'` (a gate that is not declared above in the block);
* in `lock.txt`: `bad line`, `bad name 'X'`, `bad version 'V'`, `duplicate package 'NAME'` (a features word is checked like `+FEATURE` words).

Files are read and checked in this order: `index.txt`, `project.txt`, then `lock.txt` when the command needs it.

## 4. Commands

### `keel lock [--oldest] [--fresh]`

Resolves the project (section 5). On success it prints one line per chosen package, sorted by name, in the format of `lock.txt`, then `locked N packages`, and writes the same lines to `lock.txt` (replacing it). On failure it prints one `error:` line (section 5) and leaves `lock.txt` alone. Options: `--oldest`: try the oldest candidates first instead of the newest; `--fresh`: ignore `lock.txt`. An argument starting with `-` that is not an option gives `error: unknown option 'ARG'`; any other argument gives `error: usage: keel lock [OPTION...]`.

Unless `--fresh` is given, an existing `lock.txt` is read (and must be well formed) and its versions are **preferred**: see the candidate order in section 5. A missing `lock.txt` is fine here.

### `keel upgrade NAME...`

Like `lock`, but `lock.txt` must exist (`error: cannot read lock.txt`) and every `NAME` must be locked there (`error: NAME is not locked`, for the first one that is not); the preference is taken from the lock *without* the named packages, so they are free to move to other versions while everything else stays put when possible. No arguments: `error: usage: keel upgrade NAME...`. Output as for `lock`.

### `keel tree`

Needs `lock.txt`. Prints the dependency tree of the locked packages. The first line is `root`. Below it, indented by two spaces per level, come the names wanted in `project.txt` (each once, sorted by name), and below each package the packages it needs, again each once and sorted by name. The *needs* of a locked package are those of its locked version in the index that are active given the features recorded for it in the lock (a package locked at a version missing from the index has none). A package line is `NAME VERSION` followed by ` [FEATURES]` (features joined with `,`) when features are enabled; a name that is not in the lock is printed as `NAME (not locked)` and has no children. The tree is printed depth first; a locked package that was already printed earlier in the output (anywhere above or before it) gets ` (*)` appended and is not expanded again.

### `keel check`

Needs `lock.txt`. Validates it without searching and prints one `problem:` line per violation, in this order: first for each `want` line of the project in file order, then for each locked package in name order, then (last) the packages nothing needs. The messages (`V` is a locked version, `C` a constraint as written, `NAME`/`DEP` package names):

* `problem: root wants NAME C but NAME is not locked` (and nothing more for that line); `problem: root wants NAME C but locked NAME is V` if the locked version does not satisfy `C`; then for each requested feature `F` (sorted) that is not enabled in the lock: `problem: root wants NAME +F but the lock does not enable it`.
* For a locked `NAME V`: if the index has no such version: `problem: NAME V is not in the index` (and no further check for it). For each enabled feature `F` (sorted) that the version does not declare: `problem: NAME V has no feature F`.
* For each active need of `NAME V` in file order (`needs DEP C +F...`) (a gated need is active when its gate is enabled for `NAME` in the lock): `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but DEP is not locked` (and nothing more for the need); `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but locked DEP is W` if `W` does not satisfy `C`; then for each requested feature `F` (sorted) not enabled for `DEP` in the lock: `problem: NAME V needs DEP +F but the lock does not enable it`.
* For each `breaks X C` of `NAME V` in file order: `problem: NAME V breaks X C but locked X is W` if `X` is locked at a version `W` satisfying `C`.
* A package is *used* if it is wanted by the project or needed (actively, as above) by a used locked package. `problem: NAME is locked but nothing needs it` for every locked package that is not used, in name order.

At the end: `ok: N packages` (exit status 0) when there was no problem, otherwise `FAILED: P problems` (exit status 1). Extra arguments give `error: usage: keel check`; for `tree`: `error: usage: keel tree`.

Any other command gives `error: unknown command 'WORD'`; no command gives `error: usage: keel COMMAND [ARGS]`.

## 5. Resolution

The search works on a **state**: the packages chosen so far (name -> version), for every name the list of **requirements** received in order (constraint text and who required it: `root`, or `NAME VERSION` of the package that needs it), the set of features requested for every name, the list of `breaks` recorded by chosen packages, and a **queue** of names that still need a decision, in the order they were first required.

**Start.** The state is empty. For each `want` line in file order: add the requirement `(constraint, root)` for its name, add its features to the requested ones; append the name to the queue unless it was queued before (a name is queued at most once, ever).

**Step.** Take the first name `N` of the queue (the one that has waited longest).
1. If the index has no package named `N` at all, this is a **dead end** with the message `unknown package N`.
2. Otherwise compute the **candidates**: all versions of `N` in the index, newest first, minus these:
   * yanked versions, unless the version is the one `N` has in the preferred lock (see below);
   * versions that do not satisfy *every* requirement collected for `N`;
   * versions that satisfy the constraint of a recorded `breaks` entry whose name is `N`;
   * versions that do not declare every feature requested for `N`;
   If `lock --oldest` was given, the remaining candidates are reversed (oldest first). Finally, if the preferred lock has a version for `N` and it is still a candidate, it moves to the front (the others keep their relative order).
3. Try the candidates in order. Count every try (across the whole search): when the count would exceed **3000**, the search stops at once with `error: search limit reached`. To *try* a candidate `P`: copy the state, remove `N` from the front of the queue, and **choose** `P`:
   * record `N -> P` as chosen (the requested features of `N` stay as they are);
   * for each `breaks X C` of `P` in file order: if `X` is already chosen at a version satisfying `C`, the try fails; otherwise record `(X, C)`;
   * take the **active needs** of `P`: its `needs` lines in file order, leaving out the gated ones whose feature is not requested for `N`. Process them first in, first out, each as follows (a need of a package `Q` on `DEP`):
     * append `(constraint, Q VERSION)` to the requirements of `DEP`;
     * let `NEW` be the features asked for by the need that were not requested for `DEP` yet; add them to the requested features of `DEP`;
     * if `DEP` is already chosen at version `D`: the try fails if `D` does not satisfy the constraint; or if `D` does not declare every feature in `NEW`; otherwise append to the end of the work list the gated needs of `D` (file order) whose gate is in `NEW`;
     * otherwise, if `DEP` was never queued, append it to the queue.
   If the try did not fail, continue the search from the new state (the next **Step**); if that search succeeds, its result is the answer; otherwise go on with the next candidate.
4. If all candidates failed or there were none, this is a **dead end** for `N` with the message `cannot resolve N: needs C1 (WHO1), C2 (WHO2), ...` listing *all* requirements of `N` in this state in their order, each as `CONSTRAINT (WHO)`. (If `N` has no requirements the list is empty and the message ends with `needs `; this cannot happen for queued names.) Then the search backs up to the previous choice.
When the queue is empty the search succeeds: the answer is the set of chosen packages with, for each, its requested features (the enabled features). The **first dead end** that ever occurs during the whole search gives the error line `error: ` + its message, if the search finally fails (later dead ends are ignored). The step counter does not reset when backing up.

**The preferred lock.** For `lock` without `--fresh`, the preference is every `NAME VERSION` of `lock.txt` if that file exists; for `upgrade` it is the same minus the named packages; for `lock --fresh` it is empty. A preferred version needs not satisfy anything: it only matters as described in the candidate rules (it is exempt from the yanked rule and moves to the front when it is a candidate).

prompt: Our little package ecosystem needs its own resolver, and the rules (invented, so please don't assume semver or cargo behaviour) are written up in `README.md`. The tool is `keel`; build it in Rust as `target/debug/keel`, built with `cargo build --offline` (binary crate `keel`, entry point `src/main.rs`, no dependencies). Examples can be run with `python3 tests/run_examples.py`. The hidden checks cover all four commands, every error text and a lot of resolution scenarios where the order of attempts decides the answer.

start.README.md:
# moor: a dependency resolver and lock validator

`moor` reads a package index, a project file and (optionally) a lock file from the **current directory**, decides which version of which package to use, and writes or checks a lock file. The version scheme, the constraint syntax and the way conflicts are searched are specific to this ecosystem; follow the rules below, not the conventions of any real package manager.

Build and run it as `python3 src/moor.py` (entry point `src/moor.py`; other modules go next to it in `src/`). Usage: `moor COMMAND [ARGS]`. Everything is printed to standard output (nothing on standard error matters). The exit status is `1` if any printed line starts with `error:` or `FAILED`, otherwise `0`.

## 1. Words, names, versions

Files are read as lines of text. In every file `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line; the rest of a line is split into *words* at white space; lines without words are skipped. Line numbers start at 1 and count every line, comments and empty lines included.

A **name** is a lower-case letter followed by lower-case letters, digits and `-` (package names, nothing else).

A **version** is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` where each number is `0` or has no leading zero and at most six digits. Tags are not part of this ecosystem: `1.2.3-rc1` is a bad version. Versions are ordered by the three numbers. Two versions are equal when they are equal in that order.

## 2. Constraints

A **constraint** is one word (no spaces): clauses separated by `,`, and a version must satisfy every clause. A clause is an operator and a *partial version* (`1`, `1.2` or `1.2.3`; missing numbers count as 0), or `*`, or a bare partial version, which means `=` (always allowed). Clause meanings (`V` is the partial version completed with zeros):

* `>=V`: at least `V`
* `<V`: less than `V`
* `=V`: equal to `V`
* `^V`: at least `V` and below the *next breaking number*: `(MAJOR+1).0.0` (the major number is always the breaking one, also when it is 0)
* `~V`: at least `V` and below `MAJOR.(MINOR+1).0`
* `*`: every version

The operators `>`, `<=`, `!=` do not exist in this ecosystem; a clause using one is a bad constraint.

The upper bound of `^` and `~` is compared on the three numbers only, whatever the tag: a version is below the bound when its triple is (so `^1.2` allows `1.9.9-rc1` but not `2.0.0-rc1`). All other clause comparisons (`>=`, `<`, `=` and so on) use the full version order of section 1, so `<2.0.0` *does* allow `2.0.0-rc1` and `>=1.0.0` does not allow `1.0.0-rc1`. A constraint that is empty, has an empty clause, an unknown operator or a bad partial version is a **bad constraint**.

## 3. The files

**`index.txt`** lists the available packages as blocks. A block starts with `pkg NAME VERSION` and continues with directive lines until the next `pkg` line:

* `needs NAME CONSTRAINT`: this package version needs the package `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT`.
* `breaks NAME CONSTRAINT`: this version cannot be used together with any version of `NAME` that satisfies `CONSTRAINT`.
* `yanked`: this version is withdrawn: it is never chosen, unless the lock file already holds exactly this version (see `lock`).

The same package may appear in several blocks with different versions; the same name and version twice is an error.

**`project.txt`** has one directive per line: `want NAME CONSTRAINT`: the project needs `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT`. Several lines may mention the same name.

**`lock.txt`** has one line per locked package, sorted by name: `NAME VERSION`.

**File errors.** A file that cannot be read gives `error: cannot read FILE`. A malformed line gives `error: FILE:LINE: MESSAGE` and nothing else is done; the first problem in file order wins. `MESSAGE` is one of:

* `unknown directive 'WORD'` (first word not allowed in that file; the allowed ones are `pkg`, `needs`, `yanked`, `breaks` in the index and `want` in the project);
* `'WORD' outside a package block` (an index directive before the first `pkg` line);
* `bad line` (wrong number of words for the directive);
* `bad name 'X'` (checked after the shape: the package name of `pkg`/`needs`/`breaks`/`want`);
* `bad version 'V'`, `bad constraint 'C'` (checked after the names of the same line);
* `duplicate package NAME VERSION`;
* in `lock.txt`: `bad line`, `bad name 'X'`, `bad version 'V'`, `duplicate package 'NAME'`.

Files are read and checked in this order: `index.txt`, `project.txt`, then `lock.txt` when the command needs it.

## 4. Commands

### `moor lock [--fresh]`

Resolves the project (section 5). On success it prints one line per chosen package, sorted by name, in the format of `lock.txt`, then `locked N packages`, and writes the same lines to `lock.txt` (replacing it). On failure it prints one `error:` line (section 5) and leaves `lock.txt` alone. Options: `--fresh`: ignore `lock.txt`. An argument starting with `-` that is not an option gives `error: unknown option 'ARG'`; any other argument gives `error: usage: moor lock [OPTION...]`.

Unless `--fresh` is given, an existing `lock.txt` is read (and must be well formed) and its versions are **preferred**: see the candidate order in section 5. A missing `lock.txt` is fine here.

### `moor upgrade NAME...`

Like `lock`, but `lock.txt` must exist (`error: cannot read lock.txt`) and every `NAME` must be locked there (`error: NAME is not locked`, for the first one that is not); the preference is taken from the lock *without* the named packages, so they are free to move to other versions while everything else stays put when possible. No arguments: `error: usage: moor upgrade NAME...`. Output as for `lock`.

### `moor tree`

Needs `lock.txt`. Prints the dependency tree of the locked packages. The first line is `root`. Below it, indented by two spaces per level, come the names wanted in `project.txt` (each once, sorted by name), and below each package the packages it needs, again each once and sorted by name. The *needs* of a locked package are those of its locked version in the index (a package locked at a version missing from the index has none). A package line is `NAME VERSION`; a name that is not in the lock is printed as `NAME (not locked)` and has no children. The tree is printed depth first; a locked package that was already printed earlier in the output (anywhere above or before it) gets ` (*)` appended and is not expanded again.

### `moor check`

Needs `lock.txt`. Validates it without searching and prints one `problem:` line per violation, in this order: first for each `want` line of the project in file order, then for each locked package in name order, The messages (`V` is a locked version, `C` a constraint as written, `NAME`/`DEP` package names):

* `problem: root wants NAME C but NAME is not locked` (and nothing more for that line); `problem: root wants NAME C but locked NAME is V` if the locked version does not satisfy `C`.
* For a locked `NAME V`: if the index has no such version: `problem: NAME V is not in the index` (and no further check for it).
* For each active need of `NAME V` in file order (`needs DEP C`): `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but DEP is not locked` (and nothing more for the need); `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but locked DEP is W` if `W` does not satisfy `C`.
* For each `breaks X C` of `NAME V` in file order: `problem: NAME V breaks X C but locked X is W` if `X` is locked at a version `W` satisfying `C`.

At the end: `ok: N packages` (exit status 0) when there was no problem, otherwise `FAILED: P problems` (exit status 1). Extra arguments give `error: usage: moor check`; for `tree`: `error: usage: moor tree`.

Any other command gives `error: unknown command 'WORD'`; no command gives `error: usage: moor COMMAND [ARGS]`.

## 5. Resolution

The search works on a **state**: the packages chosen so far (name -> version), for every name the list of **requirements** received in order (constraint text and who required it: `root`, or `NAME VERSION` of the package that needs it), the list of `breaks` recorded by chosen packages, and a **queue** of names that still need a decision, in the order they were first required.

**Start.** The state is empty. For each `want` line in file order: add the requirement `(constraint, root)` for its name; append the name to the queue unless it was queued before (a name is queued at most once, ever).

**Step.** Take the first name `N` of the queue (the one that has waited longest).
1. If the index has no package named `N` at all, this is a **dead end** with the message `unknown package N`.
2. Otherwise compute the **candidates**: all versions of `N` in the index, newest first, minus these:
   * yanked versions, unless the version is the one `N` has in the preferred lock (see below);
   * versions that do not satisfy *every* requirement collected for `N`;
   * versions that satisfy the constraint of a recorded `breaks` entry whose name is `N`;
   The remaining candidates stay in this order. Finally, if the preferred lock has a version for `N` and it is still a candidate, it moves to the front (the others keep their relative order).
3. Try the candidates in order. Count every try (across the whole search): when the count would exceed **2000**, the search stops at once with `error: search limit reached`. To *try* a candidate `P`: copy the state, remove `N` from the front of the queue, and **choose** `P`:
   * record `N -> P` as chosen;
   * for each `breaks X C` of `P` in file order: if `X` is already chosen at a version satisfying `C`, the try fails; otherwise record `(X, C)`;
   * take the **active needs** of `P`: its `needs` lines in file order. Process them first in, first out, each as follows (a need of a package `Q` on `DEP`):
     * append `(constraint, Q VERSION)` to the requirements of `DEP`;
     * if `DEP` is already chosen at version `D`: the try fails if `D` does not satisfy the constraint;
     * otherwise, if `DEP` was never queued, append it to the queue.
   If the try did not fail, continue the search from the new state (the next **Step**); if that search succeeds, its result is the answer; otherwise go on with the next candidate.
4. If all candidates failed or there were none, this is a **dead end** for `N` with the message `cannot resolve N: needs C1 (WHO1), C2 (WHO2), ...` listing *all* requirements of `N` in this state in their order, each as `CONSTRAINT (WHO)`. (If `N` has no requirements the list is empty and the message ends with `needs `; this cannot happen for queued names.) Then the search backs up to the previous choice.
When the queue is empty the search succeeds: the answer is the set of chosen packages. The **first dead end** that ever occurs during the whole search gives the error line `error: ` + its message, if the search finally fails (later dead ends are ignored). The step counter does not reset when backing up.

**The preferred lock.** For `lock` without `--fresh`, the preference is every `NAME VERSION` of `lock.txt` if that file exists; for `upgrade` it is the same minus the named packages; for `lock --fresh` it is empty. A preferred version needs not satisfy anything: it only matters as described in the candidate rules (it is exempt from the yanked rule and moves to the front when it is a candidate).

# davit: a dependency resolver and lock validator

`davit` reads a package index, a project file and (optionally) a lock file from the **current directory**, decides which version of which package to use, and writes or checks a lock file. The version scheme, the constraint syntax and the way conflicts are searched are specific to this ecosystem; follow the rules below, not the conventions of any real package manager.

Build and run it as `target/debug/davit`, built with `cargo build --offline` (binary crate `davit`, entry point `src/main.rs`, no dependencies). Usage: `davit COMMAND [ARGS]`. Everything is printed to standard output (nothing on standard error matters). The exit status is `1` if any printed line starts with `error:` or `FAILED`, otherwise `0`.

## 1. Words, names, versions

Files are read as lines of text. In every file `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line; the rest of a line is split into *words* at white space; lines without words are skipped. Line numbers start at 1 and count every line, comments and empty lines included.

A **name** is a lower-case letter followed by lower-case letters, digits and `-` (package names, feature names, nothing else).

A **version** is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` where each number is `0` or has no leading zero and at most six digits, optionally followed by `-TAG`, a **tag** being one or more lower-case letters followed by digits (for example `rc1`, `beta12`). Versions are ordered by the three numbers; for equal numbers a version *with* a tag is lower than the one without, and two tags are compared as plain byte strings (`rc10` < `rc2`). Two versions are equal when they are equal in that order.

## 2. Constraints

A **constraint** is one word (no spaces): clauses separated by `,`, and a version must satisfy every clause. A clause is an operator and a *partial version* (`1`, `1.2` or `1.2.3`, or `1.2.3-rc1`; missing numbers count as 0; a tag requires all three numbers), or `*`, or a bare partial version, which means `=` (always allowed). Clause meanings (`V` is the partial version completed with zeros):

* `>=V`: at least `V`
* `>V`: greater than `V`
* `<=V`: at most `V`
* `<V`: less than `V`
* `=V`: equal to `V`
* `^V`: at least `V` and below the *next breaking number*: `(MAJOR+1).0.0` if MAJOR is not 0; `0.(MINOR+1).0` if MAJOR is 0 and MINOR is not 0; `0.0.(PATCH+1)` if both are 0
* `~V`: at least `V` and below `MAJOR.(MINOR+1).0`

The operators `!=`, `*` do not exist in this ecosystem; a clause using one is a bad constraint.

The upper bound of `^` and `~` is compared on the three numbers only, whatever the tag: a version is below the bound when its triple is (so `^1.2` allows `1.9.9-rc1` but not `2.0.0-rc1`). All other clause comparisons (`>=`, `<`, `=` and so on) use the full version order of section 1, so `<2.0.0` *does* allow `2.0.0-rc1` and `>=1.0.0` does not allow `1.0.0-rc1`. A constraint that is empty, has an empty clause, an unknown operator or a bad partial version is a **bad constraint**.

## 3. The files

**`index.txt`** lists the available packages as blocks. A block starts with `pkg NAME VERSION` and continues with directive lines until the next `pkg` line:

* `needs NAME CONSTRAINT [+FEATURE...] [if FEATURE]`: this package version needs the package `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT`. `+FEATURE` words ask for features of `NAME` to be enabled. `if FEATURE` makes the need *conditional*: it is only active when `FEATURE` of this package is enabled (the feature must have been declared earlier in the same block).
* `feature NAME`: this version offers the feature `NAME` (declaring a feature twice in a block is an error).
* `yanked`: this version is withdrawn: it is never chosen, unless the lock file already holds exactly this version (see `lock`).

The same package may appear in several blocks with different versions; the same name and version twice is an error.

**`project.txt`** has one directive per line: `want NAME CONSTRAINT [+FEATURE...]`: the project needs `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT` with the given features enabled. Several lines may mention the same name.

**`lock.txt`** has one line per locked package, sorted by name: `NAME VERSION [FEATURES]`, where `FEATURES` is one word: the enabled features sorted by name and joined with `,` (omitted when none is enabled).

**File errors.** A file that cannot be read gives `error: cannot read FILE`. A malformed line gives `error: FILE:LINE: MESSAGE` and nothing else is done; the first problem in file order wins. `MESSAGE` is one of:

* `unknown directive 'WORD'` (first word not allowed in that file; the allowed ones are `pkg`, `needs`, `yanked`, `feature` in the index and `want` in the project);
* `'WORD' outside a package block` (an index directive before the first `pkg` line);
* `bad line` (wrong number of words for the directive; in `needs` and `want` the `+FEATURE` words come after the constraint);
* `bad name 'X'` (checked after the shape: the package name of `pkg`/`needs`/`breaks`/`want`, the gate of `if`, each feature of `feature` and `+FEATURE`, `X` printed without the `+`);
* `bad version 'V'`, `bad constraint 'C'` (checked after the names of the same line);
* `duplicate package NAME VERSION`, `duplicate feature 'F'`, `undeclared feature 'F'` (a gate that is not declared above in the block);
* in `lock.txt`: `bad line`, `bad name 'X'`, `bad version 'V'`, `duplicate package 'NAME'` (a features word is checked like `+FEATURE` words).

Files are read and checked in this order: `index.txt`, `project.txt`, then `lock.txt` when the command needs it.

## 4. Commands

### `davit lock [--oldest]`

Resolves the project (section 5). On success it prints one line per chosen package, sorted by name, in the format of `lock.txt`, then `locked N packages`, and writes the same lines to `lock.txt` (replacing it). On failure it prints one `error:` line (section 5) and leaves `lock.txt` alone. Options: `--oldest`: try the oldest candidates first instead of the newest. An argument starting with `-` that is not an option gives `error: unknown option 'ARG'`; any other argument gives `error: usage: davit lock [OPTION...]`.
### `davit tree`

Needs `lock.txt`. Prints the dependency tree of the locked packages. The first line is `root`. Below it, indented by two spaces per level, come the names wanted in `project.txt` (each once, sorted by name), and below each package the packages it needs, again each once and sorted by name. The *needs* of a locked package are those of its locked version in the index that are active given the features recorded for it in the lock (a package locked at a version missing from the index has none). A package line is `NAME VERSION` followed by ` [FEATURES]` (features joined with `,`) when features are enabled; a name that is not in the lock is printed as `NAME (not locked)` and has no children. The tree is printed depth first; a locked package that was already printed earlier in the output (anywhere above or before it) gets ` (*)` appended and is not expanded again.

### `davit check`

Needs `lock.txt`. Validates it without searching and prints one `problem:` line per violation, in this order: first for each `want` line of the project in file order, then for each locked package in name order, then (last) the packages nothing needs. The messages (`V` is a locked version, `C` a constraint as written, `NAME`/`DEP` package names):

* `problem: root wants NAME C but NAME is not locked` (and nothing more for that line); `problem: root wants NAME C but locked NAME is V` if the locked version does not satisfy `C`; then for each requested feature `F` (sorted) that is not enabled in the lock: `problem: root wants NAME +F but the lock does not enable it`.
* For a locked `NAME V`: if the index has no such version: `problem: NAME V is not in the index` (and no further check for it). For each enabled feature `F` (sorted) that the version does not declare: `problem: NAME V has no feature F`.
* For each active need of `NAME V` in file order (`needs DEP C +F...`) (a gated need is active when its gate is enabled for `NAME` in the lock): `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but DEP is not locked` (and nothing more for the need); `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but locked DEP is W` if `W` does not satisfy `C`; then for each requested feature `F` (sorted) not enabled for `DEP` in the lock: `problem: NAME V needs DEP +F but the lock does not enable it`.
* A package is *used* if it is wanted by the project or needed (actively, as above) by a used locked package. `problem: NAME is locked but nothing needs it` for every locked package that is not used, in name order.

At the end: `ok: N packages` (exit status 0) when there was no problem, otherwise `FAILED: P problems` (exit status 1). Extra arguments give `error: usage: davit check`; for `tree`: `error: usage: davit tree`.

Any other command gives `error: unknown command 'WORD'`; no command gives `error: usage: davit COMMAND [ARGS]`.

## 5. Resolution

The search works on a **state**: the packages chosen so far (name -> version), for every name the list of **requirements** received in order (constraint text and who required it: `root`, or `NAME VERSION` of the package that needs it), the set of features requested for every name, and a **queue** of names that still need a decision, in the order they were first required.

**Start.** The state is empty. For each `want` line in file order: add the requirement `(constraint, root)` for its name, add its features to the requested ones; append the name to the queue unless it was queued before (a name is queued at most once, ever).

**Step.** Take the first name `N` of the queue (the one that has waited longest).
1. If the index has no package named `N` at all, this is a **dead end** with the message `unknown package N`.
2. Otherwise compute the **candidates**: all versions of `N` in the index, newest first, minus these:
   * yanked versions, unless the version is the one `N` has in the preferred lock (see below);
   * versions that do not satisfy *every* requirement collected for `N`;
   * versions that do not declare every feature requested for `N`;
   If `lock --oldest` was given, the remaining candidates are reversed (oldest first). 
3. Try the candidates in order. Count every try (across the whole search): when the count would exceed **1500**, the search stops at once with `error: search limit reached`. To *try* a candidate `P`: copy the state, remove `N` from the front of the queue, and **choose** `P`:
   * record `N -> P` as chosen (the requested features of `N` stay as they are);
   * take the **active needs** of `P`: its `needs` lines in file order, leaving out the gated ones whose feature is not requested for `N`. Process them first in, first out, each as follows (a need of a package `Q` on `DEP`):
     * append `(constraint, Q VERSION)` to the requirements of `DEP`;
     * let `NEW` be the features asked for by the need that were not requested for `DEP` yet; add them to the requested features of `DEP`;
     * if `DEP` is already chosen at version `D`: the try fails if `D` does not satisfy the constraint; or if `D` does not declare every feature in `NEW`; otherwise append to the end of the work list the gated needs of `D` (file order) whose gate is in `NEW`;
     * otherwise, if `DEP` was never queued, append it to the queue.
   If the try did not fail, continue the search from the new state (the next **Step**); if that search succeeds, its result is the answer; otherwise go on with the next candidate.
4. If all candidates failed or there were none, this is a **dead end** for `N` with the message `cannot resolve N: needs C1 (WHO1), C2 (WHO2), ...` listing *all* requirements of `N` in this state in their order, each as `CONSTRAINT (WHO)`. (If `N` has no requirements the list is empty and the message ends with `needs `; this cannot happen for queued names.) Then the search backs up to the previous choice.
When the queue is empty the search succeeds: the answer is the set of chosen packages with, for each, its requested features (the enabled features). The **first dead end** that ever occurs during the whole search gives the error line `error: ` + its message, if the search finally fails (later dead ends are ignored). The step counter does not reset when backing up.

# jetty: a dependency resolver and lock validator

`jetty` reads a package index, a project file and (optionally) a lock file from the **current directory**, decides which version of which package to use, and writes or checks a lock file. The version scheme, the constraint syntax and the way conflicts are searched are specific to this ecosystem; follow the rules below, not the conventions of any real package manager.

Build and run it as `python3 src/jetty.py` (entry point `src/jetty.py`; other modules go next to it in `src/`). Usage: `jetty COMMAND [ARGS]`. Everything is printed to standard output (nothing on standard error matters). The exit status is `1` if any printed line starts with `error:` or `FAILED`, otherwise `0`.

## 1. Words, names, versions

Files are read as lines of text. In every file `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line; the rest of a line is split into *words* at white space; lines without words are skipped. Line numbers start at 1 and count every line, comments and empty lines included.

A **name** is a lower-case letter followed by lower-case letters, digits and `-` (package names, feature names, nothing else).

A **version** is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` where each number is `0` or has no leading zero and at most six digits. Tags are not part of this ecosystem: `1.2.3-rc1` is a bad version. Versions are ordered by the three numbers. Two versions are equal when they are equal in that order.

## 2. Constraints

A **constraint** is one word (no spaces): clauses separated by `,`, and a version must satisfy every clause. A clause is an operator and a *partial version* (`1`, `1.2` or `1.2.3`; missing numbers count as 0), or `*`, or a bare partial version, which means `=` (always allowed). Clause meanings (`V` is the partial version completed with zeros):

* `>=V`: at least `V`
* `<=V`: at most `V`
* `<V`: less than `V`
* `!=V`: not equal to `V`
* `^V`: at least `V` and below the *next breaking number*: `(MAJOR+1).0.0` if MAJOR is not 0; `0.(MINOR+1).0` if MAJOR is 0 and MINOR is not 0; `0.0.(PATCH+1)` if both are 0
* `*`: every version

The operators `>`, `=`, `~` do not exist in this ecosystem; a clause using one is a bad constraint.

The upper bound of `^` and `~` is compared on the three numbers only, whatever the tag: a version is below the bound when its triple is (so `^1.2` allows `1.9.9-rc1` but not `2.0.0-rc1`). All other clause comparisons (`>=`, `<`, `=` and so on) use the full version order of section 1, so `<2.0.0` *does* allow `2.0.0-rc1` and `>=1.0.0` does not allow `1.0.0-rc1`. A constraint that is empty, has an empty clause, an unknown operator or a bad partial version is a **bad constraint**.

## 3. The files

**`index.txt`** lists the available packages as blocks. A block starts with `pkg NAME VERSION` and continues with directive lines until the next `pkg` line:

* `needs NAME CONSTRAINT [+FEATURE...] [if FEATURE]`: this package version needs the package `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT`. `+FEATURE` words ask for features of `NAME` to be enabled. `if FEATURE` makes the need *conditional*: it is only active when `FEATURE` of this package is enabled (the feature must have been declared earlier in the same block).
* `feature NAME`: this version offers the feature `NAME` (declaring a feature twice in a block is an error).
* `breaks NAME CONSTRAINT`: this version cannot be used together with any version of `NAME` that satisfies `CONSTRAINT`.
* `yanked`: this version is withdrawn: it is never chosen, unless the lock file already holds exactly this version (see `lock`).

The same package may appear in several blocks with different versions; the same name and version twice is an error.

**`project.txt`** has one directive per line: `want NAME CONSTRAINT [+FEATURE...]`: the project needs `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT` with the given features enabled. Several lines may mention the same name.

**`lock.txt`** has one line per locked package, sorted by name: `NAME VERSION [FEATURES]`, where `FEATURES` is one word: the enabled features sorted by name and joined with `,` (omitted when none is enabled).

**File errors.** A file that cannot be read gives `error: cannot read FILE`. A malformed line gives `error: FILE:LINE: MESSAGE` and nothing else is done; the first problem in file order wins. `MESSAGE` is one of:

* `unknown directive 'WORD'` (first word not allowed in that file; the allowed ones are `pkg`, `needs`, `yanked`, `breaks`, `feature` in the index and `want` in the project);
* `'WORD' outside a package block` (an index directive before the first `pkg` line);
* `bad line` (wrong number of words for the directive; in `needs` and `want` the `+FEATURE` words come after the constraint);
* `bad name 'X'` (checked after the shape: the package name of `pkg`/`needs`/`breaks`/`want`, the gate of `if`, each feature of `feature` and `+FEATURE`, `X` printed without the `+`);
* `bad version 'V'`, `bad constraint 'C'` (checked after the names of the same line);
* `duplicate package NAME VERSION`, `duplicate feature 'F'`, `undeclared feature 'F'` (a gate that is not declared above in the block);
* in `lock.txt`: `bad line`, `bad name 'X'`, `bad version 'V'`, `duplicate package 'NAME'` (a features word is checked like `+FEATURE` words).

Files are read and checked in this order: `index.txt`, `project.txt`, then `lock.txt` when the command needs it.

## 4. Commands

### `jetty lock [--oldest] [--fresh]`

Resolves the project (section 5). On success it prints one line per chosen package, sorted by name, in the format of `lock.txt`, then `locked N packages`, and writes the same lines to `lock.txt` (replacing it). On failure it prints one `error:` line (section 5) and leaves `lock.txt` alone. Options: `--oldest`: try the oldest candidates first instead of the newest; `--fresh`: ignore `lock.txt`. An argument starting with `-` that is not an option gives `error: unknown option 'ARG'`; any other argument gives `error: usage: jetty lock [OPTION...]`.

Unless `--fresh` is given, an existing `lock.txt` is read (and must be well formed) and its versions are **preferred**: see the candidate order in section 5. A missing `lock.txt` is fine here.

### `jetty upgrade NAME...`

Like `lock`, but `lock.txt` must exist (`error: cannot read lock.txt`) and every `NAME` must be locked there (`error: NAME is not locked`, for the first one that is not); the preference is taken from the lock *without* the named packages, so they are free to move to other versions while everything else stays put when possible. No arguments: `error: usage: jetty upgrade NAME...`. Output as for `lock`.

### `jetty tree`

Needs `lock.txt`. Prints the dependency tree of the locked packages. The first line is `root`. Below it, indented by two spaces per level, come the names wanted in `project.txt` (each once, sorted by name), and below each package the packages it needs, again each once and sorted by name. The *needs* of a locked package are those of its locked version in the index that are active given the features recorded for it in the lock (a package locked at a version missing from the index has none). A package line is `NAME VERSION` followed by ` [FEATURES]` (features joined with `,`) when features are enabled; a name that is not in the lock is printed as `NAME (not locked)` and has no children. The tree is printed depth first; a locked package that was already printed earlier in the output (anywhere above or before it) gets ` (*)` appended and is not expanded again.

### `jetty check`

Needs `lock.txt`. Validates it without searching and prints one `problem:` line per violation, in this order: first for each `want` line of the project in file order, then for each locked package in name order, then (last) the packages nothing needs. The messages (`V` is a locked version, `C` a constraint as written, `NAME`/`DEP` package names):

* `problem: root wants NAME C but NAME is not locked` (and nothing more for that line); `problem: root wants NAME C but locked NAME is V` if the locked version does not satisfy `C`; then for each requested feature `F` (sorted) that is not enabled in the lock: `problem: root wants NAME +F but the lock does not enable it`.
* For a locked `NAME V`: if the index has no such version: `problem: NAME V is not in the index` (and no further check for it). For each enabled feature `F` (sorted) that the version does not declare: `problem: NAME V has no feature F`.
* For each active need of `NAME V` in file order (`needs DEP C +F...`) (a gated need is active when its gate is enabled for `NAME` in the lock): `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but DEP is not locked` (and nothing more for the need); `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but locked DEP is W` if `W` does not satisfy `C`; then for each requested feature `F` (sorted) not enabled for `DEP` in the lock: `problem: NAME V needs DEP +F but the lock does not enable it`.
* For each `breaks X C` of `NAME V` in file order: `problem: NAME V breaks X C but locked X is W` if `X` is locked at a version `W` satisfying `C`.
* A package is *used* if it is wanted by the project or needed (actively, as above) by a used locked package. `problem: NAME is locked but nothing needs it` for every locked package that is not used, in name order.

At the end: `ok: N packages` (exit status 0) when there was no problem, otherwise `FAILED: P problems` (exit status 1). Extra arguments give `error: usage: jetty check`; for `tree`: `error: usage: jetty tree`.

Any other command gives `error: unknown command 'WORD'`; no command gives `error: usage: jetty COMMAND [ARGS]`.

## 5. Resolution

The search works on a **state**: the packages chosen so far (name -> version), for every name the list of **requirements** received in order (constraint text and who required it: `root`, or `NAME VERSION` of the package that needs it), the set of features requested for every name, the list of `breaks` recorded by chosen packages, and a **queue** of names that still need a decision, in the order they were first required.

**Start.** The state is empty. For each `want` line in file order: add the requirement `(constraint, root)` for its name, add its features to the requested ones; append the name to the queue unless it was queued before (a name is queued at most once, ever).

**Step.** Take the first name `N` of the queue (the one that has waited longest).
1. If the index has no package named `N` at all, this is a **dead end** with the message `unknown package N`.
2. Otherwise compute the **candidates**: all versions of `N` in the index, newest first, minus these:
   * yanked versions, unless the version is the one `N` has in the preferred lock (see below);
   * versions that do not satisfy *every* requirement collected for `N`;
   * versions that satisfy the constraint of a recorded `breaks` entry whose name is `N`;
   * versions that do not declare every feature requested for `N`;
   If `lock --oldest` was given, the remaining candidates are reversed (oldest first). Finally, if the preferred lock has a version for `N` and it is still a candidate, it moves to the front (the others keep their relative order).
3. Try the candidates in order. Count every try (across the whole search): when the count would exceed **4000**, the search stops at once with `error: search limit reached`. To *try* a candidate `P`: copy the state, remove `N` from the front of the queue, and **choose** `P`:
   * record `N -> P` as chosen (the requested features of `N` stay as they are);
   * for each `breaks X C` of `P` in file order: if `X` is already chosen at a version satisfying `C`, the try fails; otherwise record `(X, C)`;
   * take the **active needs** of `P`: its `needs` lines in file order, leaving out the gated ones whose feature is not requested for `N`. Process them first in, first out, each as follows (a need of a package `Q` on `DEP`):
     * append `(constraint, Q VERSION)` to the requirements of `DEP`;
     * let `NEW` be the features asked for by the need that were not requested for `DEP` yet; add them to the requested features of `DEP`;
     * if `DEP` is already chosen at version `D`: the try fails if `D` does not satisfy the constraint; or if `D` does not declare every feature in `NEW`; otherwise append to the end of the work list the gated needs of `D` (file order) whose gate is in `NEW`;
     * otherwise, if `DEP` was never queued, append it to the queue.
   If the try did not fail, continue the search from the new state (the next **Step**); if that search succeeds, its result is the answer; otherwise go on with the next candidate.
4. If all candidates failed or there were none, this is a **dead end** for `N` with the message `cannot resolve N: needs C1 (WHO1), C2 (WHO2), ...` listing *all* requirements of `N` in this state in their order, each as `CONSTRAINT (WHO)`. (If `N` has no requirements the list is empty and the message ends with `needs `; this cannot happen for queued names.) Then the search backs up to the previous choice.
When the queue is empty the search succeeds: the answer is the set of chosen packages with, for each, its requested features (the enabled features). The **first dead end** that ever occurs during the whole search gives the error line `error: ` + its message, if the search finally fails (later dead ends are ignored). The step counter does not reset when backing up.

**The preferred lock.** For `lock` without `--fresh`, the preference is every `NAME VERSION` of `lock.txt` if that file exists; for `upgrade` it is the same minus the named packages; for `lock --fresh` it is empty. A preferred version needs not satisfy anything: it only matters as described in the candidate rules (it is exempt from the yanked rule and moves to the front when it is a candidate).

# cleat: a dependency resolver and lock validator

`cleat` reads a package index, a project file and (optionally) a lock file from the **current directory**, decides which version of which package to use, and writes or checks a lock file. The version scheme, the constraint syntax and the way conflicts are searched are specific to this ecosystem; follow the rules below, not the conventions of any real package manager.

Build and run it as `target/debug/cleat`, built with `cargo build --offline` (binary crate `cleat`, entry point `src/main.rs`, no dependencies). Usage: `cleat COMMAND [ARGS]`. Everything is printed to standard output (nothing on standard error matters). The exit status is `1` if any printed line starts with `error:` or `FAILED`, otherwise `0`.

## 1. Words, names, versions

Files are read as lines of text. In every file `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line; the rest of a line is split into *words* at white space; lines without words are skipped. Line numbers start at 1 and count every line, comments and empty lines included.

A **name** is a lower-case letter followed by lower-case letters, digits and `-` (package names, nothing else).

A **version** is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` where each number is `0` or has no leading zero and at most six digits, optionally followed by `-TAG`, a **tag** being one or more lower-case letters followed by digits (for example `rc1`, `beta12`). Versions are ordered by the three numbers; for equal numbers a version *with* a tag is lower than the one without, and two tags are compared as plain byte strings (`rc10` < `rc2`). Two versions are equal when they are equal in that order.

## 2. Constraints

A **constraint** is one word (no spaces): clauses separated by `,`, and a version must satisfy every clause. A clause is an operator and a *partial version* (`1`, `1.2` or `1.2.3`, or `1.2.3-rc1`; missing numbers count as 0; a tag requires all three numbers), or `*`, or a bare partial version, which means `=` (always allowed). Clause meanings (`V` is the partial version completed with zeros):

* `>=V`: at least `V`
* `>V`: greater than `V`
* `<=V`: at most `V`
* `<V`: less than `V`
* `=V`: equal to `V`
* `!=V`: not equal to `V`
* `^V`: at least `V` and below the *next breaking number*: `(MAJOR+1).0.0` (the major number is always the breaking one, also when it is 0)
* `~V`: at least `V` and below `MAJOR.(MINOR+1).0`
* `*`: every version

The upper bound of `^` and `~` is compared on the three numbers only, whatever the tag: a version is below the bound when its triple is (so `^1.2` allows `1.9.9-rc1` but not `2.0.0-rc1`). All other clause comparisons (`>=`, `<`, `=` and so on) use the full version order of section 1, so `<2.0.0` *does* allow `2.0.0-rc1` and `>=1.0.0` does not allow `1.0.0-rc1`. A constraint that is empty, has an empty clause, an unknown operator or a bad partial version is a **bad constraint**.

## 3. The files

**`index.txt`** lists the available packages as blocks. A block starts with `pkg NAME VERSION` and continues with directive lines until the next `pkg` line:

* `needs NAME CONSTRAINT`: this package version needs the package `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT`.
* `yanked`: this version is withdrawn: it is never chosen, unless the lock file already holds exactly this version (see `lock`).

The same package may appear in several blocks with different versions; the same name and version twice is an error.

**`project.txt`** has one directive per line: `want NAME CONSTRAINT`: the project needs `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT`. Several lines may mention the same name.

**`lock.txt`** has one line per locked package, sorted by name: `NAME VERSION`.

**File errors.** A file that cannot be read gives `error: cannot read FILE`. A malformed line gives `error: FILE:LINE: MESSAGE` and nothing else is done; the first problem in file order wins. `MESSAGE` is one of:

* `unknown directive 'WORD'` (first word not allowed in that file; the allowed ones are `pkg`, `needs`, `yanked` in the index and `want` in the project);
* `'WORD' outside a package block` (an index directive before the first `pkg` line);
* `bad line` (wrong number of words for the directive);
* `bad name 'X'` (checked after the shape: the package name of `pkg`/`needs`/`breaks`/`want`);
* `bad version 'V'`, `bad constraint 'C'` (checked after the names of the same line);
* `duplicate package NAME VERSION`;
* in `lock.txt`: `bad line`, `bad name 'X'`, `bad version 'V'`, `duplicate package 'NAME'`.

Files are read and checked in this order: `index.txt`, `project.txt`, then `lock.txt` when the command needs it.

## 4. Commands

### `cleat lock [--fresh]`

Resolves the project (section 5). On success it prints one line per chosen package, sorted by name, in the format of `lock.txt`, then `locked N packages`, and writes the same lines to `lock.txt` (replacing it). On failure it prints one `error:` line (section 5) and leaves `lock.txt` alone. Options: `--fresh`: ignore `lock.txt`. An argument starting with `-` that is not an option gives `error: unknown option 'ARG'`; any other argument gives `error: usage: cleat lock [OPTION...]`.

Unless `--fresh` is given, an existing `lock.txt` is read (and must be well formed) and its versions are **preferred**: see the candidate order in section 5. A missing `lock.txt` is fine here.

### `cleat upgrade NAME...`

Like `lock`, but `lock.txt` must exist (`error: cannot read lock.txt`) and every `NAME` must be locked there (`error: NAME is not locked`, for the first one that is not); the preference is taken from the lock *without* the named packages, so they are free to move to other versions while everything else stays put when possible. No arguments: `error: usage: cleat upgrade NAME...`. Output as for `lock`.

### `cleat tree`

Needs `lock.txt`. Prints the dependency tree of the locked packages. The first line is `root`. Below it, indented by two spaces per level, come the names wanted in `project.txt` (each once, sorted by name), and below each package the packages it needs, again each once and sorted by name. The *needs* of a locked package are those of its locked version in the index (a package locked at a version missing from the index has none). A package line is `NAME VERSION`; a name that is not in the lock is printed as `NAME (not locked)` and has no children. The tree is printed depth first; a locked package that was already printed earlier in the output (anywhere above or before it) gets ` (*)` appended and is not expanded again.

### `cleat check`

Needs `lock.txt`. Validates it without searching and prints one `problem:` line per violation, in this order: first for each `want` line of the project in file order, then for each locked package in name order, then (last) the packages nothing needs. The messages (`V` is a locked version, `C` a constraint as written, `NAME`/`DEP` package names):

* `problem: root wants NAME C but NAME is not locked` (and nothing more for that line); `problem: root wants NAME C but locked NAME is V` if the locked version does not satisfy `C`.
* For a locked `NAME V`: if the index has no such version: `problem: NAME V is not in the index` (and no further check for it).
* For each active need of `NAME V` in file order (`needs DEP C`): `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but DEP is not locked` (and nothing more for the need); `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but locked DEP is W` if `W` does not satisfy `C`.
* A package is *used* if it is wanted by the project or needed (actively, as above) by a used locked package. `problem: NAME is locked but nothing needs it` for every locked package that is not used, in name order.

At the end: `ok: N packages` (exit status 0) when there was no problem, otherwise `FAILED: P problems` (exit status 1). Extra arguments give `error: usage: cleat check`; for `tree`: `error: usage: cleat tree`.

Any other command gives `error: unknown command 'WORD'`; no command gives `error: usage: cleat COMMAND [ARGS]`.

## 5. Resolution

The search works on a **state**: the packages chosen so far (name -> version), for every name the list of **requirements** received in order (constraint text and who required it: `root`, or `NAME VERSION` of the package that needs it), and a **queue** of names that still need a decision, in the order they were first required.

**Start.** The state is empty. For each `want` line in file order: add the requirement `(constraint, root)` for its name; append the name to the queue unless it was queued before (a name is queued at most once, ever).

**Step.** Take the first name `N` of the queue (the one that has waited longest).
1. If the index has no package named `N` at all, this is a **dead end** with the message `unknown package N`.
2. Otherwise compute the **candidates**: all versions of `N` in the index, newest first, minus these:
   * yanked versions, unless the version is the one `N` has in the preferred lock (see below);
   * versions that do not satisfy *every* requirement collected for `N`;
   The remaining candidates stay in this order. Finally, if the preferred lock has a version for `N` and it is still a candidate, it moves to the front (the others keep their relative order).
3. Try the candidates in order. Count every try (across the whole search): when the count would exceed **2500**, the search stops at once with `error: search limit reached`. To *try* a candidate `P`: copy the state, remove `N` from the front of the queue, and **choose** `P`:
   * record `N -> P` as chosen;
   * take the **active needs** of `P`: its `needs` lines in file order. Process them first in, first out, each as follows (a need of a package `Q` on `DEP`):
     * append `(constraint, Q VERSION)` to the requirements of `DEP`;
     * if `DEP` is already chosen at version `D`: the try fails if `D` does not satisfy the constraint;
     * otherwise, if `DEP` was never queued, append it to the queue.
   If the try did not fail, continue the search from the new state (the next **Step**); if that search succeeds, its result is the answer; otherwise go on with the next candidate.
4. If all candidates failed or there were none, this is a **dead end** for `N` with the message `cannot resolve N: needs C1 (WHO1), C2 (WHO2), ...` listing *all* requirements of `N` in this state in their order, each as `CONSTRAINT (WHO)`. (If `N` has no requirements the list is empty and the message ends with `needs `; this cannot happen for queued names.) Then the search backs up to the previous choice.
When the queue is empty the search succeeds: the answer is the set of chosen packages. The **first dead end** that ever occurs during the whole search gives the error line `error: ` + its message, if the search finally fails (later dead ends are ignored). The step counter does not reset when backing up.

**The preferred lock.** For `lock` without `--fresh`, the preference is every `NAME VERSION` of `lock.txt` if that file exists; for `upgrade` it is the same minus the named packages; for `lock --fresh` it is empty. A preferred version needs not satisfy anything: it only matters as described in the candidate rules (it is exempt from the yanked rule and moves to the front when it is a candidate).

start.README.md:
# ballast: a dependency resolver and lock validator

`ballast` reads a package index, a project file and (optionally) a lock file from the **current directory**, decides which version of which package to use, and writes or checks a lock file. The version scheme, the constraint syntax and the way conflicts are searched are specific to this ecosystem; follow the rules below, not the conventions of any real package manager.

Build and run it as `python3 src/ballast.py` (entry point `src/ballast.py`; other modules go next to it in `src/`). Usage: `ballast COMMAND [ARGS]`. Everything is printed to standard output (nothing on standard error matters). The exit status is `1` if any printed line starts with `error:` or `FAILED`, otherwise `0`.

## 1. Words, names, versions

Files are read as lines of text. In every file `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line; the rest of a line is split into *words* at white space; lines without words are skipped. Line numbers start at 1 and count every line, comments and empty lines included.

A **name** is a lower-case letter followed by lower-case letters, digits and `-` (package names, feature names, nothing else).

A **version** is `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` where each number is `0` or has no leading zero and at most six digits, optionally followed by `-TAG`, a **tag** being one or more lower-case letters followed by digits (for example `rc1`, `beta12`). Versions are ordered by the three numbers; for equal numbers a version *with* a tag is lower than the one without, and two tags are compared as plain byte strings (`rc10` < `rc2`). Two versions are equal when they are equal in that order.

## 2. Constraints

A **constraint** is one word (no spaces): clauses separated by `,`, and a version must satisfy every clause. A clause is an operator and a *partial version* (`1`, `1.2` or `1.2.3`, or `1.2.3-rc1`; missing numbers count as 0; a tag requires all three numbers), or `*`, or a bare partial version, which means `=` (always allowed). Clause meanings (`V` is the partial version completed with zeros):

* `>=V`: at least `V`
* `>V`: greater than `V`
* `<V`: less than `V`
* `=V`: equal to `V`
* `!=V`: not equal to `V`
* `^V`: at least `V` and below the *next breaking number*: `(MAJOR+1).0.0` if MAJOR is not 0; `0.(MINOR+1).0` if MAJOR is 0 and MINOR is not 0; `0.0.(PATCH+1)` if both are 0
* `~V`: at least `V` and below `MAJOR.(MINOR+1).0`
* `*`: every version

The operators `<=` do not exist in this ecosystem; a clause using one is a bad constraint.

The upper bound of `^` and `~` is compared on the three numbers only, whatever the tag: a version is below the bound when its triple is (so `^1.2` allows `1.9.9-rc1` but not `2.0.0-rc1`). All other clause comparisons (`>=`, `<`, `=` and so on) use the full version order of section 1, so `<2.0.0` *does* allow `2.0.0-rc1` and `>=1.0.0` does not allow `1.0.0-rc1`. A constraint that is empty, has an empty clause, an unknown operator or a bad partial version is a **bad constraint**.

## 3. The files

**`index.txt`** lists the available packages as blocks. A block starts with `pkg NAME VERSION` and continues with directive lines until the next `pkg` line:

* `needs NAME CONSTRAINT [+FEATURE...] [if FEATURE]`: this package version needs the package `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT`. `+FEATURE` words ask for features of `NAME` to be enabled. `if FEATURE` makes the need *conditional*: it is only active when `FEATURE` of this package is enabled (the feature must have been declared earlier in the same block).
* `feature NAME`: this version offers the feature `NAME` (declaring a feature twice in a block is an error).
* `yanked`: this version is withdrawn: it is never chosen, unless the lock file already holds exactly this version (see `lock`).

The same package may appear in several blocks with different versions; the same name and version twice is an error.

**`project.txt`** has one directive per line: `want NAME CONSTRAINT [+FEATURE...]`: the project needs `NAME` in a version satisfying `CONSTRAINT` with the given features enabled. Several lines may mention the same name.

**`lock.txt`** has one line per locked package, sorted by name: `NAME VERSION [FEATURES]`, where `FEATURES` is one word: the enabled features sorted by name and joined with `,` (omitted when none is enabled).

**File errors.** A file that cannot be read gives `error: cannot read FILE`. A malformed line gives `error: FILE:LINE: MESSAGE` and nothing else is done; the first problem in file order wins. `MESSAGE` is one of:

* `unknown directive 'WORD'` (first word not allowed in that file; the allowed ones are `pkg`, `needs`, `yanked`, `feature` in the index and `want` in the project);
* `'WORD' outside a package block` (an index directive before the first `pkg` line);
* `bad line` (wrong number of words for the directive; in `needs` and `want` the `+FEATURE` words come after the constraint);
* `bad name 'X'` (checked after the shape: the package name of `pkg`/`needs`/`breaks`/`want`, the gate of `if`, each feature of `feature` and `+FEATURE`, `X` printed without the `+`);
* `bad version 'V'`, `bad constraint 'C'` (checked after the names of the same line);
* `duplicate package NAME VERSION`, `duplicate feature 'F'`, `undeclared feature 'F'` (a gate that is not declared above in the block);
* in `lock.txt`: `bad line`, `bad name 'X'`, `bad version 'V'`, `duplicate package 'NAME'` (a features word is checked like `+FEATURE` words).

Files are read and checked in this order: `index.txt`, `project.txt`, then `lock.txt` when the command needs it.

## 4. Commands

### `ballast lock`

Resolves the project (section 5). On success it prints one line per chosen package, sorted by name, in the format of `lock.txt`, then `locked N packages`, and writes the same lines to `lock.txt` (replacing it). On failure it prints one `error:` line (section 5) and leaves `lock.txt` alone. There are no options. An argument starting with `-` that is not an option gives `error: unknown option 'ARG'`; any other argument gives `error: usage: ballast lock [OPTION...]`.
### `ballast tree`

Needs `lock.txt`. Prints the dependency tree of the locked packages. The first line is `root`. Below it, indented by two spaces per level, come the names wanted in `project.txt` (each once, sorted by name), and below each package the packages it needs, again each once and sorted by name. The *needs* of a locked package are those of its locked version in the index that are active given the features recorded for it in the lock (a package locked at a version missing from the index has none). A package line is `NAME VERSION` followed by ` [FEATURES]` (features joined with `,`) when features are enabled; a name that is not in the lock is printed as `NAME (not locked)` and has no children. The tree is printed depth first; a locked package that was already printed earlier in the output (anywhere above or before it) gets ` (*)` appended and is not expanded again.

### `ballast check`

Needs `lock.txt`. Validates it without searching and prints one `problem:` line per violation, in this order: first for each `want` line of the project in file order, then for each locked package in name order, The messages (`V` is a locked version, `C` a constraint as written, `NAME`/`DEP` package names):

* `problem: root wants NAME C but NAME is not locked` (and nothing more for that line); `problem: root wants NAME C but locked NAME is V` if the locked version does not satisfy `C`; then for each requested feature `F` (sorted) that is not enabled in the lock: `problem: root wants NAME +F but the lock does not enable it`.
* For a locked `NAME V`: if the index has no such version: `problem: NAME V is not in the index` (and no further check for it). For each enabled feature `F` (sorted) that the version does not declare: `problem: NAME V has no feature F`.
* For each active need of `NAME V` in file order (`needs DEP C +F...`) (a gated need is active when its gate is enabled for `NAME` in the lock): `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but DEP is not locked` (and nothing more for the need); `problem: NAME V needs DEP C but locked DEP is W` if `W` does not satisfy `C`; then for each requested feature `F` (sorted) not enabled for `DEP` in the lock: `problem: NAME V needs DEP +F but the lock does not enable it`.

At the end: `ok: N packages` (exit status 0) when there was no problem, otherwise `FAILED: P problems` (exit status 1). Extra arguments give `error: usage: ballast check`; for `tree`: `error: usage: ballast tree`.

Any other command gives `error: unknown command 'WORD'`; no command gives `error: usage: ballast COMMAND [ARGS]`.

## 5. Resolution

The search works on a **state**: the packages chosen so far (name -> version), for every name the list of **requirements** received in order (constraint text and who required it: `root`, or `NAME VERSION` of the package that needs it), the set of features requested for every name, and a **queue** of names that still need a decision, in the order they were first required.

**Start.** The state is empty. For each `want` line in file order: add the requirement `(constraint, root)` for its name, add its features to the requested ones; append the name to the queue unless it was queued before (a name is queued at most once, ever).

**Step.** Take the first name `N` of the queue (the one that has waited longest).
1. If the index has no package named `N` at all, this is a **dead end** with the message `unknown package N`.
2. Otherwise compute the **candidates**: all versions of `N` in the index, newest first, minus these:
   * yanked versions, unless the version is the one `N` has in the preferred lock (see below);
   * versions that do not satisfy *every* requirement collected for `N`;
   * versions that do not declare every feature requested for `N`;
   The remaining candidates stay in this order. 
3. Try the candidates in order. Count every try (across the whole search): when the count would exceed **3500**, the search stops at once with `error: search limit reached`. To *try* a candidate `P`: copy the state, remove `N` from the front of the queue, and **choose** `P`:
   * record `N -> P` as chosen (the requested features of `N` stay as they are);
   * take the **active needs** of `P`: its `needs` lines in file order, leaving out the gated ones whose feature is not requested for `N`. Process them first in, first out, each as follows (a need of a package `Q` on `DEP`):
     * append `(constraint, Q VERSION)` to the requirements of `DEP`;
     * let `NEW` be the features asked for by the need that were not requested for `DEP` yet; add them to the requested features of `DEP`;
     * if `DEP` is already chosen at version `D`: the try fails if `D` does not satisfy the constraint; or if `D` does not declare every feature in `NEW`; otherwise append to the end of the work list the gated needs of `D` (file order) whose gate is in `NEW`;
     * otherwise, if `DEP` was never queued, append it to the queue.
   If the try did not fail, continue the search from the new state (the next **Step**); if that search succeeds, its result is the answer; otherwise go on with the next candidate.
4. If all candidates failed or there were none, this is a **dead end** for `N` with the message `cannot resolve N: needs C1 (WHO1), C2 (WHO2), ...` listing *all* requirements of `N` in this state in their order, each as `CONSTRAINT (WHO)`. (If `N` has no requirements the list is empty and the message ends with `needs `; this cannot happen for queued names.) Then the search backs up to the previous choice.
When the queue is empty the search succeeds: the answer is the set of chosen packages with, for each, its requested features (the enabled features). The **first dead end** that ever occurs during the whole search gives the error line `error: ` + its message, if the search finally fails (later dead ends are ignored). The step counter does not reset when backing up.
